Amy Carmichael
AY-mee KAR-my-kuhl
proper noun (person)
Irish missionary (1867-1951) to India, founder of the Dohnavur Fellowship and rescuer of endangered children.

📖 Biblical Definition

Amy Carmichael was an Irish missionary to India who gave fifty-five years of unbroken service, never once returning home on furlough, and who founded the Dohnavur Fellowship in south India as a refuge for children in danger. Burdened by the plight of young girls (and later boys) being given to Hindu temples for ritual prostitution, she labored at great risk to rescue them, gathering hundreds of children into a Christian family at Dohnavur where they were raised in the love of Christ. She bore the work's burdens as a spiritual mother, and after an injury spent her last twenty years largely confined to bed, from which she wrote many devotional books, including If, a searching meditation on the marks of Calvary love, and Gold by Moonlight. Her writings, marked by deep devotion to Christ crucified and a refusal of self-pity, have fed the church far beyond India. Carmichael stands in the dictionary as the rescuer of endangered children and a writer of Calvary love, who poured out a long life without reserve for the least and most vulnerable, and who taught the church that the love which counts no cost is the love that was shown at the cross.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Irish missionary (1867-1951) to India, founder of the Dohnavur Fellowship; who rescued hundreds of children from temple prostitution, served fifty-five years without furlough, and wrote devotional classics like If on Calvary love.

AMY CARMICHAEL, proper noun. Irish missionary (1867-1951) to India.

Founder of the Dohnavur Fellowship in south India.

Rescued hundreds of children from temple prostitution and danger.

Served fifty-five years in India without a single furlough home.

Author of devotional classics including If, on the marks of Calvary love.

📖 Key Scripture

Matt 18:5 — "And whoso shall receive one such little child in my name receiveth me."

Matt 18:6 — "But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea."

1 John 3:16 — "Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren."

James 1:27 — "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Carmichael's life honors the recovery of self-sacrificing love for the vulnerable and the cross-shaped love that counts no cost, against a sentimental religion that loves in word but not in deed.

expand to see more

Love-in-word correction. It is easy to profess compassion and never pay its cost. Carmichael's love was costly and concrete: she risked everything to rescue endangered children and gave a long life to raising them, refusing even the relief of furlough. The dictionary holds that real love lays down its life for others, as Christ laid down His for us (1 John 3:16); pure religion visits the fatherless in their affliction (James 1:27), and the love that costs nothing is not the love of Calvary.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the seriousness with which Christ regards the little ones. Carmichael took to heart the Lord's warning that to offend one of these little ones invites a millstone (Matt 18:6), and the promise that to receive a child in His name is to receive Him (Matt 18:5). The dictionary commends her example: care for the most vulnerable is not a sentimental add-on to the faith but near the heart of it, for in the least of these we serve the Lord Himself.
